passage: At the tea stall in the small town, Vinita puffed out her cheeks. "I'm starving! I could eat a horse!" Tejas, five, went wide-eyed. "No! Please don't eat the horse!" He ran to the cart horse standing in the lane and stood in front of it with his arms out. Vinita laughed and crouched. "It's a joke, Tejas. It means I'm very hungry. I'll just eat a samosa." He lowered his arms. "Just samosa?" "Just samosa."

qa.q: What did Vinita say she could eat?
qa.a: A horse.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when he stood in front of the horse?
qa.a: Worry and a wish to protect it, because he took her words literally. He may also have been a little scared.

qa.q: How did Vinita handle the misunderstanding well?
qa.a: She laughed kindly, crouched, explained the joke and said what she would really eat.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel about Tejas's reaction?
qa.a: Amused and a bit surprised, and then aware she should explain. 😊

grounding: Shows a young child taking an exaggeration literally and an adult gently explaining the joke.

passage: In a flat in Toronto, Chidi said, "You're driving me up the wall, Paulo!" as Paulo, six, bounced a ball. Paulo looked at the wall, then at Chidi's shoes. "Where is the wall? Are you going up?" Chidi laughed. "No. It's just something people say when they're a little tired of noise." "You're tired?" "A little. Could you bounce it outside?" "Okay."

qa.q: What was Paulo bouncing?
qa.a: A ball.

qa.q: What might Paulo have been feeling while looking at the wall?
qa.a: Probably puzzled, since Paulo took the phrase literally and asked where the wall was and whether Chidi was going up.

qa.q: How could Chidi explain the phrase kindly?
qa.a: Laugh, say it is just something people say, and state the real request directly.

qa.q: How might Chidi feel in this moment?
qa.a: A little tired of the noise but amused by the question.

grounding: Shows a young child taking a figure of speech literally and an adult explaining it gently.

passage: At the end of sports day, Shalini Ma'am sat down on the grass and groaned, “My feet are killing me!” Rashmi's eyes went wide. She ran and knelt by Shalini's shoes. “Are they hurting you? Should I call the nurse?” Shalini laughed and smiled warmly. “Oh, sweetheart, it's just a saying. My feet are only tired. They're not really killing me.” Rashmi looked at the shoes suspiciously. “Just tired?” “Just tired. Want to sit with me?” Rashmi sat, still watching the shoes.

qa.q: What did Shalini Ma'am say about her feet?
qa.a: “My feet are killing me!”

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when she ran to Shalini's shoes?
qa.a: She was worried and alarmed, taking the words literally and thinking her teacher was really hurt.

qa.q: How did Shalini help Rashmi understand?
qa.a: She smiled, used a warm tone and explained gently that it was just a saying and her feet were only tired.

qa.q: How might Shalini see Rashmi's reaction?
qa.a: She finds it sweet and caring, which is why she laughs warmly rather than making fun.

grounding: A young child takes “my feet are killing me” literally, and her teacher smiles and explains gently.

passage: I'm Vikas, Reena's uncle. On Sunday, her father came in from cycling and flopped down. “I'm starving!” Reena gasped, ran to her room, and came back holding out her last biscuit. “Eat this so you don't die, Papa!” Her father looked surprised, then smiled and took her hand. “Thank you, beta. I'm very hungry, not really starving. It's just a big way of saying it.” He broke the biscuit in half and gave it back. I don't know if she understood, but she looked relieved.

qa.q: What did Reena bring her father?
qa.a: Her last biscuit.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling when she held out her biscuit?
qa.a: She was worried and alarmed, taking “I'm starving” literally and thinking her father might die.

qa.q: What did Reena's father do that helped?
qa.a: He smiled, thanked her and gently explained that he was only very hungry, then shared the biscuit.

qa.q: How did Vikas see Reena's reaction?
qa.a: Vikas wasn't sure she understood the explanation, but noticed she looked relieved.

grounding: An uncle observes a child take “I'm starving” literally, and her father smiles and explains gently.

passage:
Monday: Parveen, tired, said, “You're driving me up the wall!” Deepika looked at the wall, then at her mother's feet. “You're not on the wall.” Parveen laughed. “It's a saying. It means I'm tired.”
Wednesday: Rain thundered. “It's raining cats and dogs!” said Parveen. Deepika ran to the window, worried. “Where?” Parveen hugged her. “No real cats. It means lots of rain.”
Friday: Deepika came in from play and announced, grinning, “I'm so hungry I could eat an elephant!” Parveen laughed, and so did she.

qa.q: What did Deepika look for at the window on Wednesday?
qa.a: Cats and dogs in the rain.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she ran to the window?
qa.a: She was worried, taking “raining cats and dogs” literally and fearing animals were falling.

qa.q: What did Parveen do each time that helped Deepika learn?
qa.a: She smiled or hugged her and explained the saying gently, signalling playfulness with her tone.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel on Friday when Deepika makes her own saying?
qa.a: She likely feels delighted and amused that Deepika has started to enjoy playing with words.

grounding: Over a week, a child takes sayings literally, and her mother explains gently until she can play with one herself.

passage:
The bus was forty minutes late and the sun was blazing on the stop. Shalini fanned herself with a folder. "I'm dying in this heat," she groaned. "And I'm starving. I could eat an elephant."

Pankaj's face crumpled. He grabbed her arm. "Don't die, Mumma! And don't eat an elephant!"

Shalini laughed and pulled him close. "Oh, sweetheart, I'm not really dying. It's just a funny way to say I'm very hot. And very hungry." She made a silly face. "No elephants, I promise."

Pankaj studied her face. "A joke?"

"A joke." She handed him a biscuit. "Share?"

qa.q: How late was the bus?
qa.a: Forty minutes late.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when his face crumpled and he grabbed her arm?
qa.a: He was most likely scared and worried, because he took "I'm dying" literally. Studying her face afterwards shows he was checking whether it was really a joke.

qa.q: How did Shalini help Pankaj understand?
qa.a: She laughed warmly, pulled him close, explained what the saying really meant, and used a silly face and a playful tone to show it was a joke.

qa.q: What would change if Shalini had just said, "Don't be silly"?
qa.a: Pankaj might still be frightened and confused, and feel foolish for not understanding.

grounding: It shows a young child taking "I'm dying" and "I could eat an elephant" literally, and an adult smiling, explaining and signalling playfulness.
